draft.title: The rise of no religion in Australia
card: The Australian census asks every household about religion every five years. The question is optional, and "No religion" is the first answer listed.
In the 2021 census, close to two in five Australians (about 39%) reported no religion. It was the most common response, ahead of Catholic.
The share has risen sharply over recent decades. In 1971 it was under 1 in 100 people, and it was about 1 in 4 by 2016.
"No religion" is a census category. It does not tell us whether a person is an atheist, an agnostic or a humanist, and some people with no religion still hold spiritual beliefs.
draft.remember: No religion is now the most common census response in Australia, and it covers a range of views.

a.q: What did the 2021 census show about religion in Australia?
opts: No religion was the most common response
Catholic was still the most common response
Fewer than one in ten reported no religion
The share with no religion fell since 2016
a.why: About 39% reported no religion, which was more than any single religion, including Catholic. The Catholic option is tempting because it was the largest religious group, but it ranked behind no religion.
a.clue: Compare the no religion share with each religion.

b.q: A news writer says everyone who ticked "No religion" in 2021 is an atheist. Why is this claim not supported by the census figure?
opts: The category includes people with differing views
The census only counts atheists as no religion
The category counts only people who left a religion
The category includes only people under 30
b.why: "No religion" is a single census answer, so it can include atheists, agnostics, humanists and people with personal spiritual beliefs. The claim treats one worldview as the whole group, but the census does not ask which view a person holds.
b.clue: Think about what a single tick box can and cannot tell us.

a.best: No religion was the most common response

b.best: The category includes people with differing views

problems.detail: The 1971 figure is wrong. In the 1971 census about 6.7% reported no religion, after an instruction to write 'none' was added. The under-1% figure belongs to 1966 and earlier.
The 2016 figure is wrong. About 30% reported no religion in 2016, close to 1 in 3, not 'about 1 in 4'. The 1 in 4 level was closer to 2011, at about 22%.
